729.title: Kunti at the river
729.hook: a frightened young mother sets her shining newborn on the river, and plants a seed the whole epic will follow
729.carry: karma: every act is a seed
729.howItsDone: Many Hindus end their worship, and some end the day, with a verse from the Bhagavata Purana (kayena vacha…) that offers all of one's actions to Narayana, a way of handing the day's seeds back to God.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, young Pritha spoke Durvasa's mantra to the rising sun, and Surya answered. The sun, greeted as a god each morning.
screen: `A MANTRA, AND THE SUN.`

segments.voice: A baby is born in secret, already dressed for battle. The Mahabharata says he's born wearing armor that's part of his own body, with bright earrings in his ears, shining like his father, the sun. Any newborn would be scandal enough for an unmarried girl in a king's house. This one glows. There's no hiding him in a corner. And his mother is still very young, still a daughter under her father's roof.
screen: `BORN IN SECRET.` → `ARMOR AND EARRINGS.` → `SHINING LIKE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Kunti's choice is quick in the telling, and heavy in the hearing. Afraid of what her family and the world will say, she places her newborn son in a basket and sets it on the river. A later book tells the scene again at length: she weeps over the basket, asks the gods of the waters, the sky and the earth to keep him safe, and says whoever finds him will be blessed to raise him. Then the current carries him away, wrapped in his father's armor. Notice the word the text chooses. It doesn't call her cruel. It calls her afraid, and lets us watch her grief. Now here's the teaching Hindus hear in this story. Karma. The word simply means action, and Hindu teaching says every action is a seed: it bears fruit, sometimes at once, sometimes years later. Karma isn't a god keeping score, or a punishment dropped from the sky. It's how actions ripen. Many teachers read the whole Mahabharata as a story of karma ripening, and Kunti's basket is one of its biggest seeds. A secret kept out of fear will grow into a man who doesn't know his mother, facing his own brothers across a field. The poem follows that seed a very long way, and it never stops grieving with Kunti while it does. Karma isn't a verdict on who she is. It's the plain truth that what she did on the riverbank will meet her again. That's why Hindu teachers ask us to take small choices seriously: not out of fear, but because a seed is still small enough to choose.

730.title: The mother downstream
730.hook: downstream, a childless charioteer and his wife pull a basket from the river and raise the boy as their own
730.carry: vatsalya: the love that raises a child
730.tomorrow: what will Karna refuse a stranger?
730.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes a small image of baby Krishna, Bal Gopal or Laddu Gopal, is woken, fed and sung to like a child: vatsalya, the parent's love the bhakti tradition learned from Yashoda. Karna, too, is often called Radheya, after the mother who raised him.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-THIRTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shining baby in a basket, and a frightened mother blessing him from the bank. Karma: every act is a seed.
screen: `KARMA: EVERY ACT IS A SEED.`

segments.voice: Downstream, a man and his wife are by the water. He's Adhiratha, a charioteer, a suta, whose work is driving and caring for the chariots of warriors. She's Radha. The text tells us they have no child. Floating toward them comes a basket. They pull it to the bank, open it, and find a baby boy, glowing, in armor and earrings. Yesterday we stood with the mother who let go. Today we stand with the parents who catch.
screen: `DOWNSTREAM: ADHIRATHA AND RADHA.` → `A BASKET ON THE WATER.` → `A BOY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Adhiratha and Radha take the boy home and raise him as their son. There's no long debate in the telling. They had no child, and here is one. They name him Vasusena, a name tied to the armor and earrings he was born with. Later the world will know him as Karna. And he's also called Radheya, son of Radha, after the woman who raised him, not the one who bore him. Years later, offered a throne and a royal family, Karna will say it himself: Radha raised him with love, and Adhiratha is his father. Hindus know this shape of story well, because God himself is given one. In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna is born to Devaki in a prison, and carried across a river by night to be raised by Yashoda in a village of cowherds. The songs belong to Yashoda: Yashoda tying him to a grinding mortar for stealing butter, Yashoda looking into his open mouth and seeing the whole universe. The bhakti tradition even names a way of loving God after her: vatsalya, love like a parent's for a child. That's why so many Hindu homes keep a small image of baby Krishna, Bal Gopal, and wake him, feed him, and sing him to sleep. In Hindu teaching, the love that raises a child is holy. Karna will carry two halves all his life, the loss from upstream and the home from downstream, and the poem keeps the second half right in his name.

If you don't pray, picture someone who took you in when they didn't have to, and remember one specific kindness, the smallest you can find. Let it sit in the chest, without needing words.

731.title: Karna gives his armor
731.hook: the boy grows up worshipping the sun, and one morning a stranger asks him for the armor he was born in
731.carry: dana: giving, even when it costs
731.tomorrow: who in the crowd knows Karna?
731.howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling Karna is remembered as Daanveer, the hero of giving; his gift of the armor to Indra is retold as the measure of keeping one's word to give, whatever it costs.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-THIRTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: a charioteer and his wife caught the basket downstream. Vatsalya: the love that raises a child.

segments.voice: Every morning the young man stands facing the sun, hands joined, praying, until the sun is high and its heat is on his back. That's Karna, grown. He doesn't know the sun is his father. And the text adds a detail: while he prays, there's nothing he will refuse a Brahmin who asks. Today a stranger comes during that hour, and asks for the one thing Karna was born wearing.
screen: `HE FACES THE SUN EACH MORNING.` → `WHILE HE PRAYS, HE REFUSES NO BRAHMIN.` → `A STRANGER COMES.`

segments.voice: The stranger is dressed as a Brahmin, a priest. But the Mahabharata lets us in on the secret: he's Indra, king of the gods, and the father of Arjuna. Indra knows that as long as Karna wears his armor and earrings, nobody can beat him, so he comes to ask for them as alms. The Adi Parva tells this scene early, beside Karna's birth, though in the story's order it comes years later. In a later book, the sun himself warns Karna in a dream that Indra is coming, and tells him to refuse. Karna answers that he can't. He's vowed to give, and he'd rather lose his life than his name for giving. So the sun tells him: then ask for Indra's dart in return. The Brahmin asks. Karna asks for the dart, a weapon that can kill one enemy, and Indra grants it. Then Karna takes a blade, cuts the armor from his own body and the earrings from his ears, and hands them over. Here's the teaching Hindus hear in it. Dana: giving, one of the oldest duties in Hindu life. The Gita calls the purest gift one given simply because giving is right, at the right time, to someone worthy, expecting nothing back. Karna's gift isn't that pure; he bargains for a weapon, and guards his name. But he keeps his vow at the cost of his own protection. That's why popular tellings call him Daanveer Karna, the hero of giving, even though he'll fight on Duryodhana's side.

segments.voice: Karna's day began facing the sun, hands joined. Then choose one small gift you'll give today, time, attention, something you own, and ask nothing back. If you don't pray, skip the water and keep the gift.

732.howItsDone: The tournament scene, with Karna's entrance and Kunti's fainting, is retold by Mahabharata storytellers and on stage, where it lets the audience see what the characters can't.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-THIRTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger asked for the armor, and Karna cut it from his body. Dana: giving, even when it costs.

segments.voice: Yesterday's scene came from further down the road; today we're back in the order of events, and Karna still wears his armor. A great arena in Hastinapura. Drona, the princes' teacher, has arranged a day for them to show the city what they've learned. The stands are packed, Kunti among the women. The cousins ride and fight and shoot, and Arjuna outshines them all, the text says, while the crowd roars. Then a sound at the gate. Someone new walks in.
screen: `A DAY TO SHOW THEIR SKILL.` → `ARJUNA OUTSHINES THEM ALL.` → `A SOUND AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: It's Karna, tall and shining, in his armor and earrings. He barely bows to the teachers. He turns to Arjuna and says, in effect: everything you've done, I'll do. And he does, one feat after another, while the crowd stares. Duryodhana is overjoyed. Here at last is someone to match the cousin he resents, and he embraces Karna like a friend. Then Karna asks to fight Arjuna, one against one. And now the story swings up into the stands. Kunti sees the armor and the earrings, and she knows. This is her son, the boy she set on the river, about to fight another of her sons. The text says she faints. Vidura has her revived with cool water and sandal paste, and she comes to and watches, unable to say a word. Everyone else in the stands sees two rivals. One person sees two brothers, and she can't tell anyone. Hindu teaching takes that view a step further. In the Bhagavad Gita, spoken in this same epic, on the field where these two will finally meet, Krishna says the wise see with an equal eye: they see the one Self, the atman, in every being, and every being in that Self. Rivals, strangers, enemies: underneath, one Self. Many teachers read Kunti's view from the stands as a small picture of that wisdom. The crowd sees sides. The mother sees family. And the Gita says that, seen truly, everyone in that arena is.

Tell us your mother and father, your royal line. A prince fights only an equal. And Karna, who has just matched every feat in the arena, has no answer to give. The text says he lowers his face.

segments.voice: Duryodhana jumps in. If Arjuna will only fight a king, then let Karna be a king. And there in the arena he has Karna crowned king of Anga. Karna, overwhelmed, asks what he can give in return. Duryodhana asks only for his friendship, and Karna gives it. Then, through the crowd, comes an old man, trembling, his cloth slipping. It's Adhiratha, the charioteer who pulled a basket from the river. And Karna, the new king, his hair still wet from the crowning, bows his head to him and greets him as his father. Adhiratha holds him and weeps. It's the moment Bhima has been waiting for. You're a charioteer's son, he says, so pick up a whip; you're not fit to fight Arjuna, or to rule Anga. Duryodhana defends his friend: the origins of heroes, like the sources of rivers, are hard to know. Then the sun sets, and the day ends with nothing settled. Now go back to that bow. Hindus have an old teaching for it. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with these words: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you, your teacher, and your guest. Matru devo bhava, pitru devo bhava. It's why Hindu children still bend to touch the feet of parents and elders, at festivals, before exams, before a big day, and receive a hand on the head and a blessing. Karna could have pretended not to know the old man. Everyone was watching. He bowed instead, and paid for it with an insult.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Karna's abandonment: a crown, a bow to the old charioteer, an insult at sunset. Pitru devo bhava: honor the one who raised you.
screen: `PITRU DEVO BHAVA.`

segments.voice: Talk in the streets of Hastinapura: people are saying Yudhishthira should be king. He's fair, he's truthful, he's Pandu's eldest. Dhritarashtra is blind, so he was passed over before; why should his line rule now? Word reaches Duryodhana, and it burns. The Mahabharata gives him a long, anguished speech to his father: if Yudhishthira takes the throne, the crown will pass down his line, and we and our children will be shut out.
screen: `THE STREETS TALK.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA SHOULD BE KING.` → `DURYODHANA BURNS.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana's plan is dressed up as a kindness. Send the Pandavas away, he tells his father, to the town of Varanavata, where a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva, is under way. Let them enjoy themselves, out of the capital, out of the people's eyes. Dhritarashtra hesitates. Pandu was good to me, he says, and the people love his sons; how can I do this? But he loves his own son, and in the end he agrees. So the old king calls his nephews in and speaks warmly of Varanavata. Yudhishthira sees the purpose behind it, the text says, but he's alone and without friends at court, and he agrees. Then Duryodhana calls a minister named Purochana and gives him the real job. Build the Pandavas a fine house out of lac and resin and other things that burn, plastered so it looks like any house. Earn their trust. And one night, while they sleep, set it on fire. Notice who makes the plot possible. The blind king, who knew it was wrong, hesitated, and said yes because the one asking was his son. Hindu teaching has a word for this. Moha: delusion, the fog of attachment, one of the six enemies within, beside anger and greed. Moha isn't too little love. It's love wrapped so tightly around what's mine that it can't see what's right. Many teachers point to the very first line of the Bhagavad Gita, spoken by this same king years later: what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? My sons, and Pandu's. His eyes were blind from birth; teachers read moha as the deeper blindness.

segments.voice: Think of someone you love so much it's hard to see them clearly: a child, a sibling, a best friend, your own team. Recall one time you took their side before you knew the facts. Don't scold yourself. The Gayatri mantra, said by Hindus every morning, asks for exactly this: a mind made clear. If you pray, ask for that. If you don't, just name the 'mine' honestly, and breathe.

segments.voice: A farewell at the edge of the city. The Pandavas and their mother are setting out for Varanavata, and an unhappy crowd has followed them out. Vidura, their uncle, walks beside Yudhishthira and says something strange, in a tongue the crowd doesn't understand, the text says, that only Yudhishthira can follow. To anyone listening, it sounds like a riddle. To Yudhishthira, it's a warning.
screen: `A FAREWELL AT THE CITY'S EDGE.` → `VIDURA SPEAKS IN A HIDDEN TONGUE.` → `A WARNING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Vidura's riddle goes something like this. There's a weapon not made of steel that can still destroy a body; whoever knows it can't be killed by it. A fire that burns a whole forest can't reach the creatures that live in holes underground. Someone who knows the roads, who can find the way by the stars, will survive. Fire, holes, roads, stars. Yudhishthira answers simply: I have understood. Later, on the road, Kunti asks what all that was about, and he tells her: Vidura was warning us of fire. Then they arrive. Varanavata welcomes them with joy. Purochana greets them warmly, and after some days moves them into the new house. Walking through it, Yudhishthira catches a smell: fat, and lac. He turns to Bhima. This house, he says, is made to burn. Who sends a warning like that? Earlier in the poem, the Mahabharata tells us who Vidura really is: Dharma himself, the god of right order, born as a man because of a sage's curse. And Yudhishthira is Dharma's son. So many teachers read this scene as dharma looking after its own: the young man who keeps to truth is warned, quietly, by the one who embodies it. Hindus carry a short line for this, from the Manusmriti: dharmo rakshati rakshitah. Dharma protects those who protect it. It doesn't promise that nothing bad happens to good people; the Pandavas are about to lose a great deal. It means that holding to what's right keeps your eyes open, and keeps you near people who'll tell you the truth, even in a riddle.

segments.voice: Many Hindus take a hard choice to an elder, the way Yudhishthira listened to Vidura. Bring one choice you're facing to mind, and ask the old question: what is dharma here, the right thing, not the easy one? If you pray, ask for the clarity to see it. Then notice the room you're in, its sounds and smells, the way Yudhishthira noticed his.
